title: us judge orders trump administration redo changes farmworker visa program 2026 08 27
text:
Aug 27 (Reuters) - A federal judge has ruled that President Donald Trump's administration violated federal law by lowering the wages of foreign farmworkers with temporary H-2A ​work visas and must revisit recent changes to the program.
U.S. District Judge Kirk Sherriff in Fresno, California, said in a decision
, opens new tab
 issued late ‌Wednesday that a U.S. Department of Labor rule adopted last October would unlawfully depress the wages of American farmworkers, and that the agency had failed to explain why the changes were necessary.
Sherriff did not strike down the rule and said doing so would be disruptive for the agricultural industry. Instead, he ordered the Labor Department to promptly revisit the ​2025 regulations and adopt a new methodology to calculate wages for workers enrolled in the H-2A visa program.
The decision came in a lawsuit ​filed last year by the United Farm Workers union and 18 individual farmworkers.
The rule
, opens new tab
 altered the way the Labor Department ⁠calculated the minimum wage that must be paid to H-2A workers, including by tying it to the 17th percentile of wages for comparable jobs. Sherriff said ​that the departure from the traditional practice of setting the wage floor at the mean pay for comparable positions in a given region would have a ​dramatic impact on pay for American workers.
The Labor Department violated federal law by adopting the changes on an emergency basis and bypassing the normal rulemaking process, said Sherriff, an appointee of Democratic former President Joe Biden.
The judge also found that a separate provision of the rule would violate federal law by allowing the value of employer-provided housing to be ​deducted from workers' wages rather than shouldered by businesses.
The department must notify employers that they may be responsible for backpay for workers from the date ​of Sherriff's decision until a revised wage rate has been set, the judge said.
The Labor Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
UFW President Teresa Romero in ‌a statement ⁠said the decision recognizes that farmworkers perform essential work and should be paid fairly.
“The government must move quickly to issue new, legal wage rates that protect the jobs and wages of local farm workers, and employers must be held accountable for paying back any difference between the new legal wage and the illegal wage rates still in effect," Romero said.
To obtain H-2A visas, employers must first certify to the Labor Department that they cannot find American workers to do ​the jobs and that hiring foreign ​labor will not depress U.S. workers' ⁠wages.
The Labor Department rule cut farmworkers’ wages by up to $7 per hour, costing workers nearly $2.5 billion a year in total, according to court filings.
Business groups largely supported the rule, and some said Sherriff's decision was disappointing and would ​sow uncertainty in the industry.
"The October rule addressed longstanding problems with a wage-setting system that has contributed to rapidly ​rising labor costs and ⁠made it increasingly difficult for growers to plan for one of their largest expenses," the International Fresh Produce Association, a trade group, said in a statement.
The case is United Farm Workers v. U.S. Department of Labor, U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, No. 1:25-cv-01614.
For the plaintiffs: Kuntal Cholera of Covington & Burling; ⁠Cecilia Langberg ​of the California Rural Legal Assistance Foundation; Lori Johnson of Farmworker Justice; Mario Martinez and Edgar ​Aguilasocho of Martinez Aguilasocho Law
For the Department of Labor: Patrick Keating of the U.S. Department of Justice
